query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing and controlling short-range ordering (SRO) at the FCC/BCC interfaces in high-entropy-alloy multilayers will moderate progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading by elevating local stacking fault energies and impeding dislocation transmission.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayer with random atomic order (RSS) at the interfaces, displaying conventional dislocation slip, formation of stacking faults, and hcp phase nucleation under load.
generation.intervention: Apply tailored thermal and compositional treatments designed to induce and control SRO specifically at the multilayer interfaces while retaining the nanoscale structure.
generation.conditions: Sustained loading (creep conditions) at constant temperatures typical of service environments, with multilayer films prepared under identical geometric and compositional conditions aside from the interface treatment.
generation.structural_mediator: Interface-specific SRO, which modifies the local stacking fault energy and creates more effective dislocation barriers.
generation.mechanism: The induced SRO increases the local stacking fault energy, which reduces the ease of partial dislocation nucleation and hcp phase formation. This leads to enhanced dislocation pile-up at the interfaces and a more controlled, gradual work-hardening response under sustained load, balancing strength with deformation tolerance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline RSS multilayers, the SRO-treated multilayers will exhibit a lower volume fraction of deformation-induced hcp phases, reduced dislocation mobility (evidenced by more pronounced pile-ups), and a more gradual transition into plastic deformation during sustained loading.
generation.baseline: Conventional FCC/BCC multilayers with random interfacial chemistry that, under sustained loading, show relatively higher dislocation transmission, faster progression of plastic deformation, and increased hcp phase formation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies specifically to nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy coatings where interface engineering can induce SRO without altering the overall multilayer architecture; results may not extend to bulk materials or systems with fundamentally different phase structures.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative relationship between the degree of induced SRO and the exact modification of stacking fault energies, as well as the interplay with other factors such as grain orientation and local strain fields, remains to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers: one set is processed to induce controlled SRO at the interfaces, and the control set retains a random atomic configuration. Subject both to identical sustained loading (creep testing) at a constant temperature and stress level.
measurements: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to quantify dislocation density, types, and pile-up configurations
X-ray diffraction or electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) to measure the volume fraction of hcp phases formed
Stress–strain curve analysis to determine work-hardening rates
Nanoindentation or atomistic simulation to assess local stacking fault energy variations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SRO-treated samples do not show statistically significant reductions in hcp phase fraction, lower effective dislocation mobility, or a more gradual work-hardening response compared to the random-interface controls, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Recently, Ding et al. synthesized FCC CoCrFeNiPd and CoCrFeNiMn HEAs. The former exhibited a higher yield strength than the latter with comparable tensile ductility. They proposed that the essential difference between these two HEAs was associated with atomic segregation and short-range ordering (SRO); both were enhanced in CoCrFeNiPd, as compared with CoCrFeNiMn. The idea was that SRO tends to create resistance to deformation/slip, leading to larger dislocation glide resistance in the more ordered CoCrFeNiPd than in CoCrFeNiMn HEAs. Theoretical work by Yin et al. suggested that the strengthening was due mainly to the large atomic/misfit volume of Pd in CoCrFeNi. Ma et al. identified a number of unusual features associated with dislocations/slips in HEAs that were related to lattice distortion and/or local chemical order. SRO also occurs in medium-entropy alloys (MEAs). The atomic structure of a CoCrNi MEA indicates that Cr favors Ni and Co neighbors, reducing the electrical and thermal conductivities and increasing the stacking-fault energies and hardness.

In the plastic stage, due to the different orientation of each grain, the resolved shear stress along the slip direction of the grains, being in a favorable orientation, reached the critical value earlier, and plastic deformation occurred. The sample began to yield, which means that dislocations started to occur and continued along the slip planes, generating double-layer HCP structures in the form of intrinsic stacking fault (ISF) (Figure 4 black arrows). It indicated that dislocation slipping and grain boundary sliding dominated the primary plastic behavior. When the surrounding grains have different orientations, the dislocations cannot cross the grain boundaries and thus pile up at the grain boundaries []. A high fraction of hcp-coordinated atoms appears in the fcc grain and manifest in the form of SF, hcp phase, and twin boundary (TB). The morphology of these hcp-type structures varies from one grain to another, indicating grain orientation dependence of deformation substructures (to be discussed later). reading.lever: Introduce and control SRO at FCC/BCC multilayer interfaces to regulate dislocation transmission.
reading.why: Prior studies show SRO strengthens related HEA systems by modifying stacking fault energies and dislocation behavior, a strategy not yet applied to FCC/BCC multilayers.
